description_full: Ryanair Holdings plc, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the provision of scheduled-passenger airline services in Ireland, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, and internationally. It offers various ancillary services; engages in other activities connected with its air passenger service, including non-flight scheduled and Internet-related services, as well as in-flight sale of beverages, food, duty-free, and merchandise; and markets car hire, travel insurance, and accommodation services through its website and mobile app. The company also provides passenger and aircraft handling, ticketing, and maintenance and repair services; and markets car parking, fast-track, airport transfers, attractions, and activities on its website and mobile app, as well as sells gift vouchers. Ryanair Holdings plc was incorporated in 1996 and is headquartered in Swords, Ireland.

financial_summary: Ryanair Holdings plc is a large-cap industrials business with a $29.9B market cap on $14.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +39% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 9% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $2.0B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.12× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 23× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 6.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 11% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.00x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 17% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market.
About $79.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 54% in the 2022 bear market and 57% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 31% below its DCF fair value of $83.27, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 2%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $68.98 to $102 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 14.5 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 8.4 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 15.3 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 16% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $68.20 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.07).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.12x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 7pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.2B.
The current ratio of 0.74 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 39.0% over 3 years and 9.7% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 80%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.2% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 17.4% on average.
Analysts expect 14.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 41%.
It returns 6.7% a year to shareholders (5.2% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
people: With about 35,000 employees, each generates about $418K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 8.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $56K of free cash flow per employee.
